With over 15 years of clinical experience, Vamsee Krishna P emphasised early detection, proper medical care, and avoiding self-medication to combat the mosquito-borne illness. Dengue is a viral infection caused by a flavivirus with four distinct serotypes DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4, primarily transmitted by day-biting Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Secondary infection with a different serotype significantly increases the risk of severe dengue. Initial signs appear 4 to 10 days after a mosquito bite, including sudden high fever up to 104 deg F, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, intense muscle and joint pain, and skin rash. The critical phase occurs around days 3 to 7 as fever subsides, during which blood vessels may leak fluid, causing dangerous blood pressure drops. Warning signs requiring emergency care include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, and extreme fatigue, which often surface just as the initial fever drops. Treatment relies strictly on supportive care through rest and hydration, as no specific antiviral or antibiotic medication exists. Fever and pain must be managed using paracetamol, while aspirin and ibuprofen must be strictly avoided due to increased bleeding risks. Prevention involves clearing stagnant water weekly from pots, buckets, and coolers, wearing long-sleeved clothing, applying safe insect repellents, and using window screens or bed nets. Vaccines like Qdenga, available in endemic regions, will soon be available in India. Regarding platelet transfusions, Vamsee Krishna P clarified that transfusions are reserved strictly for patients with active bleeding or critically low counts under 10000 to 20000 per microlitre. Routine prophylactic transfusions for stable patients are avoided because transfused platelets degrade quickly in active dengue, carrying risks like fluid overload, allergic reactions, and lung injury, while most patients recover counts naturally. Hospitalisation is essential if patients experience severe stomach tenderness, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, black tarry stool, extreme weakness, cold clammy skin, breathing difficulty, fever lasting past five days, rapid platelet drops, or when living far from medical monitoring. Highlighting that one bite brings multiple health risks, Vamsee Krishna P advised immediate consultation upon noticing symptoms to ensure a safe monsoon. supplementary_news.content: Citrus County confirms first case of locally acquired Dengue fever Updated Sat, August 22, 2026 at 10:19 PM UTC CITRUS COUNTY, Fla. (WFLA) — The Florida Department of Health in Citrus County announced Saturday its first confirmed case of Dengue fever. According to the DOH, Dengue can present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash. There are usually no respiratory symptoms. Health officials said Dengue fever is not contagious but is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Symptoms appear within 15 days after being bitten. Eight cases were confirmed in Hillsborough County , with two additional cases reported in Pinellas County. DOH is coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts with Citrus County Mosquito Control through treatments such as increased truck fogging, aerial larviciding and localized ground inspections for breeding locations. Health officials encouraged the community to avoid mosquito bites by taking basic precautions such as wearing protective clothing and applying insect repellents registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. DOH also said to repair damaged screening on windows, doors, porches, and patios. Drain water from garbage cans, buckets, or any other containers where sprinkler or rainwater has collected. supplementary_news.content_title: Mosquito control officials warn it may be just a matter of time before dengue fever reaches Kern County
supplementary_news.content: Some Kern County scientists and mosquito-abatement professionals are acknowledging that dengue fever, a mosquito-borne illness also known as "breakbone fever," will likely be seen in locally acquired cases in Kern County. Mark Dery, scientific program director at Kern Mosquito Abatement & Vector Control District, told The Californian in an email that Aedes aegypti, the newest local mosquito discovered in Kern a dozen years ago, is "firmly established in Kern County," meaning the potential exists for travel cases to result in local transmission. Travel-associated cases are contracted in another country or region where dengue is common, then brought home by the traveler, while local transmission cases (locally acquired) are caught from infected mosquitoes within the local area. "With dengue infections being relatively common in many parts of the world, it is likely that California will continue to have periodic outbreaks of local dengue transmission," Dery said, referring to locally acquired cases that first began in Southern California in 2023. Despite the arrival of dengue in the Golden State, overall risk of infection remains low and it is unlikely that dengue will become established in California, Dery said. According to records compiled by the California Department of Public Health, Kern County had one travel-related dengue case last year, and none so far this year. Statewide, there were 200 travel-related cases reported last year, and 23 reported so far in 2026. Last year there were six locally transmitted cases confirmed in Los Angeles County and one in Imperial County, the CDPH reported. "I would say that it is a matter of when, and not if, there (will be) a locally transmitted case of dengue in Kern County," Dery said. "With the vector (Aedes mosquitoes) widely present, every travel case is a roll of the dice for local transmission and it will happen eventually." Travel-associated cases of dengue fever have been verified in other San Joaquin Valley counties, including Fresno, San Joaquin and Tulare counties, but so far, there are no verified cases of locally acquired dengue in the Central Valley. All local transmission cases in the state to date have been confined to Southern California. While about half the people who get the virus experience no symptoms, the illness can be quite painful and even fatal for some. Older adults, children, people with weakened immune systems and those with certain underlying health conditions are at greater risk of severe illness. Curtis Skidgel, manager of Westside Mosquito & Vector Control District in Taft, agrees that Kern will likely see local cases of the dengue virus. "I don't want to say anything that's going to scare the public, but it's very possible that a new disease, just like West Nile virus ... these things come in and out in waves." "If you've traveled somewhere that might have this disease and you're coming back and feeling sick, that's something that's really important," Skidgel said. "The mosquitoes don't come here infected. They bite somebody who's infected, or an animal that's infected, and then spread it to the population." It's important for travelers to know about these risks before they travel, so they can take preventative measures. And those who develop symptoms should talk to a healthcare provider and to make sure the provider knows about any recent travel. Infected persons should protect against further mosquito bites so that new mosquitoes don't transmit dengue to other people. The best way to protect yourself is to prevent mosquito bites altogether. Remove standing water around your home, use an EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants outdoors, and limit outdoor activity during dawn and dusk when mosquitoes are most active. While the mosquito-to-human and human-to-mosquito cycle is the primary way dengue virus is spread, researchers in 2018 found evidence that female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transmit the dengue virus to their offspring and infected male mosquitoes pass along the virus to females when they mate. And a new study published by The Lancet Regional Health Americas identifies California as "an emerging center of transmission risk in the continental USA" for dengue — and reserchers found that "approximately 18.2 million California residents may be at risk ... with an additional 4.1 million potentially at risk by mid-century under a moderate scenario of warming and urban expansion." Curtis Skidgel, manager of Westside Mosquito & Vector Control District in Taft, said at a news conference in May that changing weather patterns have been lengthening mosquito season in Kern County. Summer, he said, is beginning earlier in the spring and ending later in the fall, and that means biting mosquitoes are living longer and remaining active longer. March 2026, for example, was the warmest March on record in Bakersfield since record keeping began in the 1890s. "Warmer temperatures likely do impact activity later in the year, as mosquitoes will develop faster with warmer temperatures and will remain active for longer," said Kern Mosquito's Dery. "Further effects of increased temperature brought about by climate change could decrease mosquito development times and the incubation times of mosquito-transmitted diseases." supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Latest News PEZA achieves 72% of target with Php 216.46-B investment City hall reiterates exemptions as Baguio creatives raise amusement tax concerns Int’l plastic modellers lauded; July declared as scale modeling month in Baguio Green building code approved on second reading; proposed to curb overdevelopment Measure bolstering city’s STI, HIV, AIDS response approved on second reading Anti-distracted walking ordinance expanded with ‘keep right’ rule PEZA achieves 72% of target with Php 216.46-B investment City hall reiterates exemptions as Baguio creatives raise amusement tax concerns Int’l plastic modellers lauded; July declared as scale modeling month in Baguio Green building code approved on second reading; proposed to curb overdevelopment Measure bolstering city’s STI, HIV, AIDS response approved on second reading Anti-distracted walking ordinance expanded with ‘keep right’ rule Home News Regions Lifestyle Sports AP News Opinion Gallery Menu Home News Regions Lifestyle Sports AP News Opinion Gallery Search for: Search About Us Thursday, August 27, 2026 News Baguio dengue cases reach 543; peak expected in late August August 24, 2026 Baguio City has recorded 543 dengue cases since January 2026, with local health officials expecting the number to peak toward the last week of August before cases begin to decline around mid-October. The City Health Services Office (CHSO) provided the update during the Baguio City Council’s regular session on August 17, 2026. Representatives from the CHSO, Baguio General Hospital (BGH), and the Department of Health (DOH) were called to the session to discuss the city’s dengue situation and COVID-19 cases simultaneously. CHSO Head Celia Brillantes and City Epidemiology Surveillance Unit Head Donabel Panes said the city’s monitoring and data gathering in previous years have helped them identify the usual pattern of dengue cases, allowing them to anticipate the seasonal increase. From 2025 to 2026, the CHSO recorded a total of 1,657 dengue cases, including seven deaths. The cases included 833 males and 823 females, with 553 admitted patients. At the time of the discussion, nine patients were admitted and none had severe dengue. The CHSO clarified that the number of patients served by Baguio’s health facilities does not necessarily represent the number of dengue cases among Baguio residents. Of the more than 1,000 cases recorded in the two-year period, about 540 were Baguio residents, while the rest came from neighboring municipalities that also rely on the city’s health facilities. The CHSO also reported that dengue testing kits remain available at health centers, stressing that early detection remains important in preventing deaths, particularly because most dengue cases can be managed when patients seek medical attention early. Health officials explained that dengue cases tend to rise every three years. Weather conditions affect the mosquito population, with relative humidity, temperature, and rainfall influencing mosquito breeding. Intermittent rain can leave water in containers and other areas where mosquitoes breed, while continuous heavy rain may wash away these breeding sites. As another possible measure against dengue, the city is looking into the use of Wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacteria that can be introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, the main mosquitoes that transmit dengue. When mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia mate, the bacteria can reduce the ability of the mosquitoes to transmit dengue to people. According to the CHSO, Baguio is being considered by project proponents as a possible model for Wolbachia implementation that could eventually be expanded to other parts of the country. The city is still working on the necessary logistics and permits, and implementation will depend on approval from the DOH. A dengue vaccine is also not yet available for use in the country as it is still awaiting approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Health officials clarified that the vaccine under consideration is different from Dengvaxia. For now, the CHSO urges residents to continue following the DOH’s dengue prevention measures including the 4S strategy of searching for and destroying mosquito breeding places, securing self-protection, seeking early consultation, and supporting fogging or spraying in hotspot areas when warranted. The city is also still procuring dengue medicines for 2026. Medicines remain available, but health officials said they are hoping for faster procurement to ensure sufficient supplies. Meanwhile, DOH data showed 4,436 dengue cases across the Cordillera Administrative Region from January to August 8, 2026. Cases increased by 9% in Abra, 23% in Benguet, 44% in Ifugao, and 34% in Kalinga, while other areas including Baguio recorded decreases. – Baguio City – Sangguniang Panlungsod Share Article Related Posts PEZA achieves 72% of target with Php 216.46-B investment August 26, 2026 City hall reiterates exemptions as Baguio creatives raise amuseme ... supplementary_news.content: Pasco County confirms case of dengue fever The Florida Department of Health in Pasco County issued a mosquito advisory Tuesday afternoon after confirming a human case of dengue fever. Pasco is now the fourth county in the Tampa Bay area to acquire the mosquito-borne illness in August, following Citrus, Hillsborough and Pinellas. Health officials issued an advisory reminding residents to take "drain and cover" precautions to reduce mosquito production and protect themselves. The advisory says DOH-Pasco and Pasco County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts. What is dengue fever? Dengue fever is a viral disease spread to people through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The most common symptom of the illness is a fever — hence its name — typically presenting like the flu, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Other common symptoms include aches and pains, nausea and vomiting, headaches, and a rash. The CDC says aches and pains typically occur behind the eyes and in the muscle joints and bones. DOH-Pasco says dengue can become severe within just a few hours. Officials urge you to keep an eye out for warning signs like blood in your nose, mouth, stool or vomit, belly pain and tenderness, restlessness, irritability and lethargy. For more information on the disease, visit the CDC website

supplementary_news.content_title: Locally Acquired Dengue Fever Case Confirmed In Citrus County
supplementary_news.content: CITRUS COUNTY, Fla. – Citrus County health officials have confirmed a case of locally acquired dengue fever, prompting local agencies to step up mosquito control and surveillance operations across the area. The Florida Department of Health in Citrus County (DOH-Citrus) announced the case and confirmed it is coordinating response efforts alongside Citrus County Mosquito Control. Planned measures include increased truck fogging, aerial larviciding, and targeted ground inspections to locate and treat mosquito breeding grounds. Dengue is not spread directly from person to person. Instead, the virus is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito, with symptoms typically showing up within 14 to 15 days of a bite. According to health officials, the infection usually presents as a flu-like illness marked by fever, severe muscle aches, joint pain, and occasionally a rash. Unlike many common viral infections, dengue generally does not cause respiratory symptoms. To lower the risk of infection, DOH-Citrus advises residents to take standard precautions against mosquito bites. These steps include wearing loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants, as well as applying EPA-registered insect repellents to exposed skin and clothing. Health officials noted that EPA-registered repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, including for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Residents are also urged to eliminate standing water around their properties. Mosquitoes breed in standing water, so officials recommend draining birdbaths, flowerpots, buckets, garbage cans, pool covers, coolers, toys, and any other containers that collect rain or sprinkler runoff. Homeowners should also inspect and repair torn window, door, and patio screens to keep mosquitoes outside. The state health department maintains ongoing surveillance for multiple mosquito-borne illnesses across Florida, including dengue, malaria, chikungunya, West Nile virus, St. Louis encephalitis, and Eastern equine encephalitis. As part of statewide monitoring, residents are asked to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Mosquito: Source: TFP File Photo Public health guidance on mosquito bite prevention is available in English, Spanish, and Creole through the Department of Health’s website and its weekly surveillance reports. Anyone experiencing symptoms consistent with dengue is advised to contact a healthcare provider. supplementary_news.content_title: Dengue fever cases rise in Tampa Bay as health officials target disease-carrying mosquitoes
supplementary_news.content: TAMPA, Fla. — Health officials across the Tampa Bay area are stepping up mosquito control efforts as the number of locally acquired dengue fever cases continues to rise. Hillsborough County says it recorded its first positive dengue fever test from an insect monitoring trap in July. Since then, 30 people have been confirmed to have contracted dengue fever from local mosquito bites, while another 21 preliminary tests are showing positive results. The county is targeting areas where health officials believe dengue-carrying mosquitoes are most active, using helicopters, trucks and crews equipped with backpack sprayers. On Monday night, three helicopters treated about 30,000 acres in an area east of the I-4 and I-275 corridor, where officials said they believe some of the first local cases were concentrated. The goal is to reduce populations of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the species mostly responsible for transmitting dengue fever. But mosquito control officials say eliminating mosquitoes is only part of the effort. Gabriela Henderson with Hillsborough County Mosquito Services said Aedes aegypti mosquitoes are daytime biters, putting people who spend extended periods outdoors at risk. Health officials recommend wearing long pants and long sleeves and using mosquito repellent when spending time outside. Unlike illnesses such as the flu or COVID-19, dengue fever does not spread directly from person to person. “It is only spread through the bite of a mosquito,” Henderson said. A mosquito can become infected after biting a person who already has the virus and then transmit dengue when it bites another person. Hillsborough County Mosquito Services is also focusing on tire shops, which can provide ideal breeding conditions for Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The mosquitoes can lay eggs in small amounts of standing water, making items such as discarded tires potential breeding sites. Officials are also asking residents to eliminate standing water around their homes. That includes checking sports equipment, garbage cans, children’s toys, tools and other outdoor items that can collect rainwater. Most people infected with dengue experience mild-to-moderate illness and recover on their own, health officials said. Symptoms can include fever, vomiting, body aches and skin rashes. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that about one in 20 people who become sick with dengue develop severe dengue, which can require hospitalization. Severe cases can cause internal bleeding, organ failure and other life-threatening complications. Reducing mosquito breeding grounds and taking precautions against mosquito bites can help limit the spread of dengue in the Tampa Bay area, health officials said

By: Anthony Romano Posted 6:14 PM, Aug 22, 2026 CITRUS COUNTY, Fla. — Health officials have confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue in Citrus County, according to the Florida Department of Health (DOH) in Citrus County. DOH-Citrus said it is coordinating with Citrus County Mosquito Control to increase surveillance and prevention efforts, including truck fogging, aerial larviciding and inspections for mosquito breeding areas, according to a news release. Dengue is a mosquito-borne illness that can cause flu-like symptoms including fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and rash. Symptoms typically appear within 15 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Officials said dengue is not contagious person-to-person and is spread through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito, per the release. Health officials are urging residents to take precautions to avoid mosquito bites, including wearing long sleeves and pants, using EPA-registered insect repellents and removing standing water around homes. The Department of Health said it continues statewide monitoring for mosquito-borne illnesses including West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria, chikungunya and dengue. Residents experiencing symptoms are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider. DismissOpt out Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information ✕ Welcome! to timesofindia.comSign in / Register TOI INDTOI USTOI GCC TOI+ Home TOI Games Top Headlines India City News Photos Business World Cup Entertainment Movie Reviews Lifestyle Podcasts Elections Web Series Sports TV Food Travel Events World Music Astrology Videos Tech Auto Education Log Out Follow Us On Download App News Videos India World City Gadgets Now Auto Life & Style Entertainment Astro Business Tech TOI Games Cricket Sports TV Web Series Education Speaking Tree Relationships TOI Newsletters Health Real Estate Legal Defence Women Dengue count rises to 147 in state, Gurgaon tally 24 City | Ipsita Pati | Aug 26, 2026, 00:38 IST The state has so far reported no confirmed dengue deaths this year Comments Share Gurgaon: The city is among Haryana’s biggest dengue hotspots this season. Tired of too many ads?go ad free now Jhajjar and the city have accounted for more than a third of the 147 cases reported across the state so far. Across Haryana, 87 of the 147 cumulative cases have been reported by govt hospitals and 60 by private hospitals. According to the latest state vector-borne disease bulletin, Jhajjar has reported the highest number of cases at 28, followed by the city with 24. Together, the two districts account for 52 cases, or about 35% of the state’s total. The state has so far reported no confirmed dengue deaths this year. Five patients were still admitted to hospitals as of Aug 20, while 57 patients who had required hospitalisation had been discharged. Another 85 cases were treated on an outpatient basis. According to experts, warm and humid weather over the past few weeks was favourable for the breeding of Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit the dengue virus. Commonly seen symptoms of dengue include fever, headache, muscle and joint pain and a characteristic skin rash. Doctors emphasised the need for taking preventive measures to slow the spread of infections. They recommend wearing full-sleeved clothes, using mosquito repellents and cleaning any pools of stagnant water from containers, coolers, etc. Tired of too many ads?go ad free now Associate director of internal medicine at CK Birla Hospital (Gurgaon) Dr Tushar Tayal told TOI, “The overall number of patients presenting with dengue remains within the expected range and we have not observed an unusual increase in the severity of illness. We will need to monitor the situation over the coming weeks to determine whether there is any sustained rise in cases or severity.” The 2026 tally is currently much lower than previous years. Haryana reported 2,626 dengue cases in 2025, 6,469 in 2024 and 8,083 in 2023. This year, Karnal, with 13 cases, is the third worst-affected district. Hisar, Rewari and Sonipat have reported nine cases each, while Charkhi Dadri, Mahendragarh and Panchkula have recorded seven each. Faridabad has reported six cases so far, while Fatehabad and Panipat have recorded four each. Yamunanagar has reported four cases and Jind and Rohtak have three each. Kurukshetra has two cases, while Ambala has one. Bhiwani, Kaithal, Nuh and Palwal have not reported any cases so far.
